subject: social_studies
name: Historical Argument with Evidence Structure
problemType: Students string quotes together without analytical reasoning
targetMisconception: Belief that more quotes equal stronger arguments
teacherMoves: Model evidence sandwich (claim-evidence-analysis-connection) with historical examples (HLP Explicit Instruction)
Demonstrate selecting evidence strategically for analytical purpose (UDL 3.2)
Provide transition and analysis stems emphasizing interpretation over quotation (UDL 5.3)
Guide revision for analysis depth (HLP Feedback)
studentTasks: Select evidence that directly supports claim
Frame quote or paraphrase with context
Analyze significance beyond summary
Connect evidence to broader argument
Peer evaluate for analysis depth
supports: Model paragraphs with strong analysis (HLP Exemplars)
fadePlan: Phase 1: Teacher models complete evidence integration → Phase 2: Students use structured organizer with prompts → Phase 3: Students construct with analysis checklist → Phase 4: Independent evidence integration
whenNotToUse: When practicing document identification or when building basic comprehension skills

subject: social_studies
name: Artifact Analysis Investigation Protocol
problemType: Students don't know how to learn from physical and visual artifacts
targetMisconception: Belief that artifacts are just objects rather than historical evidence
teacherMoves: Teach artifact analysis as historical method (HLP Explicit Instruction)
Model systematic observation before interpretation (UDL 6.1)
Practice connecting artifacts to historical context (UDL 3.2)
Build from observation to interpretation to questions (UDL 6.2)
studentTasks: Observe artifact carefully and document observations
Analyze construction, materials, and condition
Interpret purpose and significance
Connect to historical context
Generate questions for further investigation
fadePlan: Phase 1: Teacher models with shared artifact → Phase 2: Guided analysis with prompts → Phase 3: Independent analysis with framework → Phase 4: Automatic artifact analysis habits
whenNotToUse: When artifacts are fragile and hands-on analysis is not possible. Use high-quality images instead.

subject: social_studies
name: Source Bias Detection and Analysis Framework
problemType: Students don't recognize bias in sources or dismiss sources with bias entirely
targetMisconception: Belief that biased sources are useless rather than requiring critical analysis
teacherMoves: Teach that all sources have perspective and potential bias (HLP Explicit Instruction)
Model identifying types of bias (UDL 3.2)
Practice using biased sources critically (UDL 8.3)
Connect bias analysis to source use (UDL 7.2)
studentTasks: Identify potential biases based on source origin and purpose
Look for evidence of bias: word choice, emphasis, omission
Assess how bias might affect source reliability
Determine what can and cannot be learned from biased source
Use source appropriately given its biases
fadePlan: Phase 1: Teacher models bias detection with explicit examples → Phase 2: Guided bias analysis with feedback → Phase 3: Independent bias detection → Phase 4: Automatic critical source evaluation
whenNotToUse: When working with neutral/balanced sources or when focus is on other skills.

subject: social_studies
name: Black History and Perspectives Integration
problemType: Black history is taught separately rather than integrated throughout curriculum
targetMisconception: Belief that Black history is supplementary rather than central to American history
teacherMoves: Center Black perspectives throughout content not just designated months (UDL 7.3)
Use Black sources and scholars (HLP Explicit Instruction)
Examine how Black peoples are represented in traditional sources (UDL 3.2)
Connect to contemporary issues and movements (UDL 7.2)
studentTasks: Identify Black perspectives in and absent from sources
Seek out Black voices on topics being studied
Analyze how representation affects understanding
Connect historical content to contemporary Black experiences
Reflect on responsibility for accurate inclusion
supports: Black source and scholar finding guide (UDL 7.3)
fadePlan: Phase 1: Teacher provides Black sources and models integration → Phase 2: Guided source seeking with support → Phase 3: Independent perspective integration → Phase 4: Automatic Black perspective seeking
whenNotToUse: Never - Black perspectives should be integrated throughout. Adjust approach based on content and context.

subject: social_studies
name: Cause and Effect Chain Analysis
problemType: Students identify simple causes without recognizing complexity
targetMisconception: Belief that historical events have single clear causes
teacherMoves: Teach multiple causation and causal chains (HLP Explicit Instruction)
Model tracing causes back through time (UDL 3.2)
Practice distinguishing proximate and ultimate causes (UDL 6.2)
Connect to contingency and counterfactuals (UDL 8.3)
studentTasks: Identify proximate (immediate) cause of event
Trace chain of causes backward in time
Identify ultimate (root) causes
Analyze how causes interact and compound
Consider what might have changed outcomes
fadePlan: Phase 1: Teacher models complete causal chain analysis → Phase 2: Guided chain building with prompts → Phase 3: Independent causal analysis → Phase 4: Automatic complex causal thinking
whenNotToUse: When simple causation is appropriate for content or learning level.

subject: social_studies
name: Historical Change and Continuity Analysis
problemType: Students focus only on change without seeing continuity or vice versa
targetMisconception: Belief that history is linear progress or that nothing really changes
teacherMoves: Model analyzing both change and continuity with attention to whose experience matters (HLP Explicit Instruction)
Demonstrate periodizing based on change and continuity analysis (UDL 3.2)
Provide framework centering experiences often absent from narratives of change (UDL 7.2)
Guide evaluating pace and extent of change (HLP Feedback)
studentTasks: Identify what changed and what continued over time period
Analyze whose experience is reflected in change and continuity patterns
Evaluate pace and extent of changes
Connect patterns to broader historical forces
Draw conclusions about transformation and persistence
supports: Model analyses centering diverse experiences (HLP Exemplars)
fadePlan: Phase 1: Teacher models complete change and continuity analysis → Phase 2: Students analyze with structured templates → Phase 3: Students use abbreviated framework → Phase 4: Independent analysis
whenNotToUse: When time period is too short for meaningful change analysis or when building foundational chronology

subject: social_studies
name: Strategic Civic Action Planning
problemType: Students want to act but lack strategic planning skills
targetMisconception: Belief that passion alone creates effective civic action
teacherMoves: Model strategic action planning with realistic goal-setting (HLP Explicit Instruction)
Demonstrate analyzing tactics for effectiveness and accessibility (UDL 3.2)
Provide framework for action rooted in community organizing traditions (UDL 7.2)
Guide reflection on action and adjustment (HLP Feedback)
studentTasks: Define specific measurable achievable goals
Analyze available resources and constraints
Select tactics matching goals and context
Plan timeline with checkpoints
Reflect on action and adjust strategy
supports: Model action plans from diverse movements (HLP Exemplars)
fadePlan: Phase 1: Teacher models complete action planning → Phase 2: Students plan with structured templates → Phase 3: Students use abbreviated framework → Phase 4: Independent action planning
whenNotToUse: When action is not possible or appropriate or when building foundational civic knowledge

subject: social_studies
name: Contemporary Civic Issue Analysis Framework
problemType: Students don't apply historical and social science thinking to current issues
targetMisconception: Belief that current events are fundamentally different from history and require no analysis
teacherMoves: Connect historical thinking to contemporary issues (HLP Explicit Instruction)
Model applying analysis frameworks to current events (UDL 6.1)
Practice finding multiple perspectives on issues (UDL 7.3)
Connect to civic responsibility and action (UDL 7.2)
studentTasks: Identify civic issue and stakeholders
Research multiple perspectives and evidence
Apply historical and social science analysis frameworks
Evaluate policy options and trade-offs
Connect analysis to potential civic action
fadePlan: Phase 1: Teacher guides analysis of selected issue → Phase 2: Structured analysis of student-chosen issue → Phase 3: Independent issue analysis → Phase 4: Ongoing civic analysis habits
whenNotToUse: When issue is too politically divisive without appropriate preparation and norms.

subject: social_studies
name: Civil Discourse Skill Development
problemType: Students can't discuss controversial topics productively
targetMisconception: Belief that disagreement must be avoided or that aggressive debate is productive
teacherMoves: Teach civil discourse as democratic skill (HLP Explicit Instruction)
Establish norms for productive disagreement (UDL 8.3)
Practice with progressively challenging topics (UDL 8.3)
Connect to democratic citizenship (UDL 7.2)
studentTasks: Learn components of civil discourse
Practice respectful disagreement with support
Engage with controversial topics using learned skills
Give and receive feedback on discourse quality
Reflect on civil discourse growth
fadePlan: Phase 1: Teacher establishes norms and models with safe topics → Phase 2: Practice with moderate topics and coaching → Phase 3: Challenging topics with established norms → Phase 4: Natural civil discourse habits
whenNotToUse: When topic is personally painful for students present without appropriate support.

subject: social_studies
name: Historical Claim-Evidence-Reasoning Structure
problemType: Students state claims without systematic evidence and reasoning support
targetMisconception: Belief that historical claims are opinions rather than evidence-based arguments
teacherMoves: Model complete CER structure with historical examples (HLP Explicit Instruction)
Demonstrate selecting evidence strategically for claims (UDL 3.2)
Provide reasoning stems connecting evidence to historical concepts (UDL 5.3)
Guide peer evaluation for CER completeness (HLP Feedback)
studentTasks: Develop specific historically arguable claim
Select evidence directly supporting claim
Explain reasoning connecting evidence to claim
Peer evaluate for CER alignment
Revise based on feedback
fadePlan: Phase 1: Teacher models complete CER → Phase 2: Students construct with structured organizer → Phase 3: Students use abbreviated stems → Phase 4: Independent CER construction
whenNotToUse: When building basic content knowledge or when claim is not arguable

subject: social_studies
name: Community-Based Research Methods
problemType: Students rely solely on internet sources without engaging community knowledge
targetMisconception: Belief that academic sources are more valid than community expertise
teacherMoves: Model designing research that honors and centers community knowledge (HLP Explicit Instruction)
Demonstrate ethical community engagement practices (UDL 3.2)
Provide framework for reciprocal community research relationships (UDL 7.2)
Guide synthesizing community and academic sources (HLP Feedback)
studentTasks: Identify community knowledge holders and resources
Design ethical research approach with community input
Conduct research using appropriate methods
Synthesize community and academic knowledge
Share findings in ways that benefit community
supports: Model research projects honoring diverse communities (HLP Exemplars)
fadePlan: Phase 1: Teacher models community research design → Phase 2: Students design with structured ethics guidance → Phase 3: Students conduct with method support → Phase 4: Independent community research
whenNotToUse: When community access is not possible or when research ethics training is insufficient

subject: social_studies
name: Comparative Historical Analysis Framework
problemType: Students describe similarities and differences without meaningful comparison
targetMisconception: Belief that comparison means listing parallel facts rather than analyzing patterns
teacherMoves: Teach comparison as analytical tool (HLP Explicit Instruction)
Model developing comparison criteria based on purpose (UDL 3.2)
Practice analysis that explains differences and similarities (UDL 6.2)
Build comparative arguments (UDL 5.3)
studentTasks: Develop comparison criteria based on analytical purpose
Gather comparable information across cases
Analyze patterns of similarity and difference
Explain why similarities and differences exist
Draw conclusions from comparative analysis
fadePlan: Phase 1: Teacher provides criteria and models analysis → Phase 2: Guided comparison with developed criteria → Phase 3: Independent comparative analysis → Phase 4: Automatic comparative thinking
whenNotToUse: When single-case depth is more important than comparison.

subject: social_studies
name: Historical Comparison Across Time and Place
problemType: Students list similarities and differences without analyzing significance
targetMisconception: Belief that comparison is about finding obvious similarities and differences
teacherMoves: Model meaningful comparison that illuminates historical understanding (HLP Explicit Instruction)
Demonstrate selecting comparison criteria based on analytical purpose (UDL 3.2)
Provide framework for comparison that respects cultural context (UDL 7.2)
Guide drawing conclusions from comparison analysis (HLP Feedback)
studentTasks: Identify cases and analytical purpose for comparison
Develop comparison criteria based on purpose
Analyze similarities and differences with cultural context
Explain significance of patterns
Draw conclusions connecting to broader historical understanding
supports: Model comparisons from diverse contexts (HLP Exemplars)
fadePlan: Phase 1: Teacher models complete comparison → Phase 2: Students compare with structured templates → Phase 3: Students develop criteria with abbreviated guidance → Phase 4: Independent comparison
whenNotToUse: When cases lack meaningful connection or when building foundational content knowledge

subject: social_studies
name: Historical Contextualization Paragraph
problemType: Students begin arguments without establishing historical setting
targetMisconception: Belief that contextualization means repeating the prompt or giving general background
teacherMoves: Model connecting specific historical developments to prompt topic (HLP Explicit Instruction)
Demonstrate moving from broad context to specific relevance (UDL 3.2)
Provide contextualization formula with examples from multiple eras (UDL 3.3)
Scaffold transition from context to thesis (UDL 5.3)
studentTasks: Identify relevant historical developments preceding or surrounding topic
Select 2-3 specific contextual factors
Draft contextualization using time-place-significance structure
Connect context explicitly to thesis
Peer evaluate for specificity and relevance
supports: Model paragraphs from various periods (HLP Exemplars)
fadePlan: Phase 1: Teacher models complete contextualization → Phase 2: Students use formula with specific prompts → Phase 3: Students construct with transition guidance only → Phase 4: Independent contextualization
whenNotToUse: When task is narrowly focused on document skills or when time constraints prevent adequate development
formativeChecks: - Context is historically accurate and specific
- Relevance to prompt topic is explicit

subject: social_studies
name: Continuity and Change Over Time Analysis
problemType: Students focus on change without recognizing continuity or vice versa
targetMisconception: Belief that history is either constant change or basically unchanging
teacherMoves: Teach continuity and change as complementary concepts (HLP Explicit Instruction)
Model identifying what changed AND what stayed the same (UDL 3.2)
Practice analysis across different time scales (UDL 6.2)
Connect to understanding historical significance (UDL 7.2)
studentTasks: Identify what changed between two time points
Identify what remained continuous
Analyze why some things changed while others persisted
Assess significance of changes relative to continuities
Draw conclusions about pace and nature of change
fadePlan: Phase 1: Teacher models with explicit both/and analysis → Phase 2: Guided analysis with matrix → Phase 3: Independent continuity-change analysis → Phase 4: Automatic balanced analysis
whenNotToUse: When focus is specifically on a single change or a single continuity.

subject: social_studies
name: Cross-Document Corroboration Analysis
problemType: Students analyze documents in isolation without cross-referencing
targetMisconception: Belief that each document is separate evidence rather than part of evidentiary web
teacherMoves: Model finding corroborating and contradicting evidence across documents (HLP Explicit Instruction)
Demonstrate evaluating stronger vs weaker corroboration (UDL 3.2)
Provide matrix tool for tracking evidence patterns (UDL 3.3)
Guide analysis of why sources might agree or disagree (HLP Feedback)
studentTasks: Identify key claims in each document
Find corroborating evidence across documents
Identify contradictions and explain possible reasons
Rate strength of corroboration
Write synthesis statement based on pattern analysis
fadePlan: Phase 1: Teacher models full corroboration analysis → Phase 2: Students use pre-filled matrix with guidance → Phase 3: Students create matrix with analysis prompts → Phase 4: Independent corroboration analysis
whenNotToUse: When documents are from single perspective or when building basic document comprehension
formativeChecks: - Matrix accurately captures agreements and contradictions

subject: social_studies
name: Economic Cost-Benefit Analysis Framework
problemType: Students calculate costs and benefits without considering who bears each
targetMisconception: Belief that aggregate benefits justify any distribution of costs
teacherMoves: Model analyzing distribution of costs and benefits across groups (HLP Explicit Instruction)
Demonstrate identifying hidden or externalized costs (UDL 3.2)
Provide framework for centering equity in economic analysis (UDL 7.2)
Guide weighing quantifiable and non-quantifiable factors (HLP Feedback)
studentTasks: Identify all costs including hidden and externalized
Identify all benefits including non-economic
Analyze distribution across different groups
Weigh using explicit value framework
Make recommendation with equity considerations
fadePlan: Phase 1: Teacher models complete cost-benefit analysis → Phase 2: Students analyze with structured templates → Phase 3: Students use abbreviated framework → Phase 4: Independent cost-benefit analysis
whenNotToUse: When economic concepts are too advanced or when practicing other analytical skills

subject: social_studies
name: Counterargument and Historical Complexity
problemType: Students present one-sided arguments without acknowledging alternatives
targetMisconception: Belief that strong arguments avoid mentioning opposing views
teacherMoves: Model identifying legitimate counterarguments in historical debates (HLP Explicit Instruction)
Demonstrate concession-refutation structure that strengthens main argument (UDL 3.3)
Provide examples of complexity acknowledgment from diverse perspectives (UDL 7.2)
Guide balance between counterargument and refutation (HLP Feedback)
studentTasks: Identify strongest opposing interpretation
Draft concession statement acknowledging validity
Develop refutation using evidence
Integrate counterargument without weakening thesis
Peer evaluate for complexity without confusion
fadePlan: Phase 1: Teacher models full counterargument integration → Phase 2: Students identify and address with structured stems → Phase 3: Students develop with balance checklist → Phase 4: Independent complexity integration
whenNotToUse: When building foundational argumentative skills or when time prevents adequate counterargument development

subject: social_studies
name: Strategic Document Grouping for DBQ
problemType: Students list documents randomly without analytical organization
targetMisconception: Belief that documents should be addressed in order presented
teacherMoves: Model multiple grouping strategies (chronological thematic perspective-based) with same document set (UDL 3.2)
Think-aloud choosing grouping based on prompt demands (HLP Explicit Instruction)
Provide categorization criteria examples from diverse historical contexts (UDL 7.2)
Guide reflection on grouping rationale (HLP Feedback)
studentTasks: Identify 2-3 possible grouping criteria for document set
Create visual map of groupings
Justify grouping choice based on prompt requirements
Evaluate peer groupings for coherence
Articulate how grouping strengthens argument
supports: Model groupings from multiple time periods (HLP Exemplars)
fadePlan: Phase 1: Teacher demonstrates three grouping approaches → Phase 2: Students choose from provided grouping criteria → Phase 3: Students develop own criteria with rationale → Phase 4: Independent strategic grouping
whenNotToUse: When document set is very small (2-3 documents) or documents share single clear theme
formativeChecks: - Grouping reflects analytical category not surface features

subject: social_studies
name: Outside Evidence Integration for DBQ
problemType: Students cannot identify or integrate relevant historical knowledge beyond documents
targetMisconception: Belief that DBQ answers should only use provided documents
teacherMoves: Model identifying relevant background knowledge from course content (HLP Explicit Instruction)
Demonstrate integrating outside evidence without overshadowing documents (UDL 3.3)
Provide content connection maps linking documents to broader historical context (UDL 3.2)
Scaffold evidence integration with sentence structures (UDL 5.3)
studentTasks: Brainstorm course content related to DBQ topic
Evaluate which outside knowledge strengthens argument
Draft integration sentences connecting outside evidence to document claims
Peer review for relevance and proportion
Revise to balance documents and outside evidence
fadePlan: Phase 1: Teacher models brainstorming and integration → Phase 2: Students use structured brainstorm with integration frames → Phase 3: Students brainstorm independently with integration checklist → Phase 4: Independent evidence integration
whenNotToUse: When DBQ is skills-focused practice emphasizing document analysis only or when students lack necessary background content
formativeChecks: - Integration strengthens rather than replaces document analysis
- Balance between documents and outside knowledge is appropriate

subject: social_studies
name: DBQ Thesis Construction from Documents
problemType: Students struggle to synthesize documents into arguable claims
targetMisconception: Belief that a thesis simply restates the question or summarizes sources
teacherMoves: Model deconstructing DBQ prompt into analytical components (UDL 3.2)
Demonstrate moving from document groupings to arguable claim (HLP Explicit Instruction)
Provide thesis formula with examples from multiple perspectives (UDL 3.3)
Conference on thesis drafts with revision prompts (HLP Feedback)
studentTasks: Analyze prompt for key historical terms and task verbs
Group documents by perspective or theme
Draft thesis using claim-because-evidence structure
Peer critique thesis for arguability and specificity
Revise thesis incorporating feedback
supports: Sample thesis bank with annotations (HLP Exemplars)
fadePlan: Phase 1: Teacher models full thesis construction with think-aloud → Phase 2: Students use formula with guided prompts → Phase 3: Students construct with checklist only → Phase 4: Independent thesis writing
whenNotToUse: When students lack basic document comprehension skills or when prompt is simple identification task
formativeChecks: - Thesis meets arguability criteria on checklist
- Peer identifies specific claim and reasoning
- Student articulates how documents support thesis

subject: social_studies
name: Deliberative Discussion Protocol
problemType: Students debate to win rather than deliberate to understand
targetMisconception: Belief that the goal of discussion is to convince others rather than to learn together
teacherMoves: Teach deliberation as distinct from debate (HLP Explicit Instruction)
Establish norms for productive disagreement (UDL 8.3)
Model listening to understand before responding (UDL 6.1)
Connect deliberation to democratic citizenship (UDL 7.2)
studentTasks: Prepare for deliberation with research and reflection
Listen to understand all perspectives
Ask clarifying questions before critiquing
Seek common ground and remaining differences
Reflect on how perspectives shifted through deliberation
fadePlan: Phase 1: Teacher facilitates with explicit process modeling → Phase 2: Student-facilitated with coaching → Phase 3: Independent deliberation → Phase 4: Natural deliberative discussion habits
whenNotToUse: When topic is too controversial without proper preparation or when quick decision is needed.

subject: social_studies
name: Disability History and Perspectives Integration
problemType: Disability history is absent or framed through deficit lens
targetMisconception: Belief that disability history is specialized topic rather than central to human experience
teacherMoves: Center disability perspectives in content (UDL 7.3)
Use disability scholars and self-advocates (HLP Explicit Instruction)
Examine how disabled peoples are represented in sources (UDL 3.2)
Connect to disability rights movement and contemporary issues (UDL 7.2)
studentTasks: Identify disability perspectives in and absent from sources
Seek out disability studies scholarship
Analyze representation and erasure in historical record
Connect historical content to contemporary disability rights
Reflect on social model of disability in historical context
supports: Representation analysis with social model lens (UDL 6.2)
fadePlan: Phase 1: Teacher provides disability sources and models integration → Phase 2: Guided source seeking with support → Phase 3: Independent perspective integration → Phase 4: Automatic disability perspective seeking
whenNotToUse: Never - disability perspectives should be integrated throughout. Adjust approach based on content and context.

subject: social_studies
name: Document-Based Question Success Framework
problemType: Students struggle with DBQ format and document integration
targetMisconception: Belief that DBQs are about using all documents rather than making arguments
teacherMoves: Teach DBQ as argument supported by selected documents (HLP Explicit Instruction)
Model document selection and integration (UDL 6.1)
Practice thesis development that drives document use (UDL 3.2)
Build stamina for extended writing (UDL 6.4)
studentTasks: Analyze documents for argument-relevant evidence
Develop thesis that documents can support
Select most useful documents for argument
Integrate documents into coherent essay
Use contextualization and synthesis as taught
fadePlan: Phase 1: Teacher models complete DBQ process → Phase 2: Guided practice with component support → Phase 3: Independent practice with feedback → Phase 4: Automatic DBQ success strategies
whenNotToUse: When practicing other historical writing formats or when time is insufficient for DBQ length.

subject: social_studies
name: Document Corroboration and Cross-Referencing
problemType: Students accept single-source claims without seeking confirmation
targetMisconception: Belief that one source is sufficient evidence for historical claims
teacherMoves: Teach corroboration as historical thinking habit (HLP Explicit Instruction)
Model comparing multiple sources on same event (UDL 3.2)
Practice identifying agreement and disagreement across sources (UDL 6.2)
Connect to reliability assessment (UDL 7.2)
studentTasks: Identify claims that need corroboration
Locate additional sources on same topic
Compare accounts across multiple sources
Assess which claims are well-supported
Draw conclusions based on corroborated evidence
fadePlan: Phase 1: Teacher provides multiple sources and guides comparison → Phase 2: Students find corroborating sources with guidance → Phase 3: Independent source seeking and comparison → Phase 4: Automatic corroboration habit
whenNotToUse: When only one source exists or when teaching single-source close reading skills.

subject: social_studies
name: Economic Indicator Critical Interpretation
problemType: Students accept economic indicators as objective measures of wellbeing
targetMisconception: Belief that GDP growth or unemployment rates capture complete economic picture
teacherMoves: Model analyzing what indicators measure and miss (HLP Explicit Instruction)
Demonstrate connecting indicators to lived economic experiences (UDL 3.2)
Provide framework for centering community economic realities (UDL 7.2)
Guide evaluating policies using multiple indicators (HLP Feedback)
studentTasks: Research how indicator is calculated and defined
Analyze what indicator captures and omits
Compare indicator to community economic experiences
Evaluate policy claims based on indicator critically
Propose additional measures for fuller picture
supports: Model analyses from diverse economic contexts (HLP Exemplars)
fadePlan: Phase 1: Teacher models complete indicator analysis → Phase 2: Students analyze with structured templates → Phase 3: Students compare with abbreviated guidance → Phase 4: Independent indicator interpretation
whenNotToUse: When economic data literacy is too limited or when indicators are straightforward

subject: social_studies
name: Economic Policy Evaluation with Equity Lens
problemType: Students evaluate policies on efficiency alone without equity analysis
targetMisconception: Belief that economic efficiency is the primary or only evaluation criterion
teacherMoves: Model multi-criteria policy evaluation including efficiency and equity (HLP Explicit Instruction)
Demonstrate applying different evaluation frameworks to same policy (UDL 3.2)
Provide framework centering affected communities in evaluation (UDL 7.2)
Guide position development with transparent value framework (HLP Feedback)
studentTasks: Identify policy goals and mechanisms
Evaluate effectiveness for stated goals
Analyze distribution of benefits and burdens
Consider community perspectives on policy
Develop position with explicit value rationale
fadePlan: Phase 1: Teacher models complete policy evaluation → Phase 2: Students evaluate with structured templates → Phase 3: Students use abbreviated framework → Phase 4: Independent policy evaluation
whenNotToUse: When policy is too complex or when building foundational economic concepts

subject: social_studies
name: Economic Reasoning Foundation Building
problemType: Students don't apply economic thinking to personal and civic decisions
targetMisconception: Belief that economics is only about money and is too complicated
teacherMoves: Teach core economic concepts accessibly (HLP Explicit Instruction)
Model applying economic reasoning to everyday decisions (UDL 7.2)
Practice cost-benefit and trade-off analysis (UDL 8.3)
Connect to personal and civic contexts (UDL 7.2)
studentTasks: Learn core economic concepts: scarcity, opportunity cost, incentives
Apply economic reasoning to personal decisions
Analyze trade-offs in policy choices
Evaluate economic arguments in media
Connect economic thinking to civic participation
supports: Economic concepts with plain language definitions (UDL 3.3)
fadePlan: Phase 1: Teacher introduces concepts with relatable examples → Phase 2: Guided application to scenarios → Phase 3: Independent economic analysis → Phase 4: Automatic economic reasoning
whenNotToUse: When economic analysis requires more background than available time allows.

subject: social_studies
name: Geographic Data Visualization and Communication
problemType: Students create maps without considering audience or message
targetMisconception: Belief that data visualization is neutral transmission of information
teacherMoves: Model designing visualizations for specific audiences and purposes (HLP Explicit Instruction)
Demonstrate ethical considerations in data representation (UDL 3.2)
Provide framework for creating visualizations that honor community data sovereignty (UDL 7.2)
Guide peer feedback on clarity and ethics (HLP Feedback)
studentTasks: Identify data message and audience
Select visualization type appropriate to purpose
Design visualization with attention to ethics and equity
Gather peer feedback on effectiveness and representation
Revise based on feedback and reflection
supports: Model visualizations from diverse contexts (HLP Exemplars)
fadePlan: Phase 1: Teacher models complete visualization design → Phase 2: Students design with structured templates → Phase 3: Students create with abbreviated guidance → Phase 4: Independent visualization design
whenNotToUse: When technical skills are too limited or when building foundational data literacy

subject: social_studies
name: Geographic Reasoning Skill Development
problemType: Students don't use geographic thinking to understand human patterns
targetMisconception: Belief that geography is just about memorizing locations
teacherMoves: Teach geographic thinking as analysis tool (HLP Explicit Instruction)
Model asking geographic questions: location, place, human-environment interaction, movement, region (UDL 3.2)
Practice applying geographic concepts to content (UDL 8.3)
Connect geography to current issues (UDL 7.2)
studentTasks: Apply five themes of geography to content
Analyze spatial patterns in human activity
Examine human-environment interactions
Use maps to develop and test hypotheses
Connect geographic thinking to current issues
fadePlan: Phase 1: Teacher models geographic thinking with explicit themes → Phase 2: Guided application with prompts → Phase 3: Independent geographic analysis → Phase 4: Automatic geographic thinking lens
whenNotToUse: When geographic analysis is not relevant to learning goals.

subject: social_studies
name: Government and Legal Document Analysis
problemType: Students struggle with dense language and assume government documents are neutral
targetMisconception: Belief that official documents represent objective truth rather than policy choices
teacherMoves: Model parsing complex language into accessible meaning (HLP Explicit Instruction)
Demonstrate identifying stakeholders and interests behind official language (UDL 3.2)
Provide vocabulary support for legal and bureaucratic terminology (UDL 2.1)
Guide analysis of intended versus actual effects (HLP Feedback)
studentTasks: Paraphrase key provisions in accessible language
Identify who benefits and who is harmed
Analyze what document reveals about power relationships
Compare stated purpose with implementation context
Use government evidence with critical framing
supports: Model analyses of diverse government sources (HLP Exemplars)
fadePlan: Phase 1: Teacher models complete government document analysis → Phase 2: Students analyze with vocabulary support and structured prompts → Phase 3: Students use analysis framework independently → Phase 4: Independent government document analysis
whenNotToUse: When document language is inaccessible even with support or when building foundational reading skills

subject: social_studies
name: Historical Claim-Evidence-Reasoning Writing
problemType: Students make historical claims without sufficient evidence or reasoning
targetMisconception: Belief that stating a conclusion is the same as making a historical argument
teacherMoves: Teach CER structure for historical arguments (HLP Explicit Instruction)
Model using evidence from primary sources (UDL 6.1)
Practice reasoning that connects evidence to claims (UDL 3.2)
Build complexity through multiple evidence points (UDL 6.2)
studentTasks: Construct clear historical claim answering the question
Select relevant evidence from sources
Write reasoning connecting evidence to claim
Address potential counterevidence
Evaluate argument strength using rubric
fadePlan: Phase 1: Full template with all prompts → Phase 2: Template with reduced prompts → Phase 3: Outline format only → Phase 4: Independent historical argument writing
whenNotToUse: When brainstorming or during evidence gathering phase.

subject: social_studies
name: Historical Contextualization Framework
problemType: Students interpret historical events through present-day lens without considering context
targetMisconception: Belief that people in the past thought and acted just like people today
teacherMoves: Teach contextualization as essential historical thinking (HLP Explicit Instruction)
Model researching context before judging historical actions (UDL 3.2)
Practice identifying what people at the time could know and believe (UDL 6.2)
Guard against presentism explicitly (UDL 7.3)
studentTasks: Research the time period context for event or source
Identify what knowledge, beliefs, and options were available then
Consider how context shaped decisions and actions
Write analysis that accounts for historical context
Reflect on how context changes interpretation
fadePlan: Phase 1: Teacher provides context and models its use → Phase 2: Guided context research → Phase 3: Independent contextualization → Phase 4: Automatic contextual thinking
whenNotToUse: When analyzing contemporary events where present context is appropriate.

subject: social_studies
name: Historical Empathy Development Practice
problemType: Students judge historical figures by modern standards without understanding their context
targetMisconception: Belief that understanding historical perspectives means agreeing with historical actions
teacherMoves: Teach historical empathy as understanding not endorsing (HLP Explicit Instruction)

subject: social_studies

subject: social_studies

subject: social_studies

fadePlan: Phase 1: Teacher models complete significance evaluation → Phase 2: Students evaluate with structured criteria → Phase 3: Students analyze perspectives with abbreviated guidance → Phase 4: Independent significance evaluation

subject: social_studies

subject: social_studies
